questions.stem: Which is the best research question for a Biology investigation?
options: What happens to plants of all kinds when they are watered with salty water?
Is salt good or bad for the growth and health of plants and animals in general?
Why do farmers in Queensland worry so much about salt in their farm soils?
How does salt concentration affect the germination rate of mung bean seeds?
questions.explanation: A good research question is specific and names both the independent variable (salt concentration) and the dependent variable (germination rate) for a defined organism. The other questions are too broad to test in one investigation, or ask about opinions rather than a measurable relationship.

questions.stem: Which statement is a testable hypothesis?
options: Light is the single most important factor for every living thing found on planet Earth
If light intensity increases, then the rate of transpiration in bean plants will increase
Transpiration is the loss of water vapour through the stomata of a plant's leaves
Light intensity and transpiration rate in bean plants will be measured over five days
questions.explanation: A hypothesis predicts a relationship between an independent and a dependent variable that can be tested by collecting data. A definition or a description of the method is not a prediction, and a sweeping claim about every living thing cannot be tested in one investigation.

questions.stem: In a Student's t-test comparing two groups, what does the null hypothesis state?
options: The data from both groups lie close to a single straight line of best fit
There is no significant difference between the means of the two groups
The means of the two groups differ by more than their standard deviations
The independent variable causes all of the change in the dependent variable
questions.explanation: The null hypothesis is the assumption of no difference between the group means. The t-test calculates how likely the observed difference would be if the null hypothesis were true.

questions.stem: Which pairing of investigation type and example is correct?
options: Experimental: recording which bird species visit a park feeder each morning
Correlational: describing every stage of a frog's life cycle in close detail
Descriptive: changing the temperature to measure its effect on enzyme activity
Comparative: measuring leaf length of one species growing in sun and in shade
questions.explanation: A comparative investigation compares a variable between groups or conditions that already exist, such as sun and shade leaves. Recording visitors and describing a life cycle are descriptive, and deliberately changing temperature is experimental.

questions.stem: A doctor writes a detailed report on one patient who had a rare reaction to a medicine. Which type of investigation is this?
options: Comparative
Case study
Experimental
Correlational
questions.explanation: A case study is an in-depth investigation of a single individual, group or event. Nothing is manipulated and no relationship between variables is measured across many subjects.

questions.stem: Why does a student set up five Petri dishes for each treatment instead of one?
options: Replicates make the independent variable easier to measure in each dish
Replicates guarantee that the results will support the student's hypothesis
Replicates reduce the effect of random variation and make the results more reliable
Replicates remove the systematic error caused by an incubator set to the wrong temperature
questions.explanation: Replicates allow a mean to be calculated, which reduces the influence of random variation between dishes, and show whether results are consistent. Repeating with the same faulty incubator would repeat any systematic error, not remove it.

questions.stem: A pH probe that has not been calibrated gives every reading 0.3 units too high. Which type of error is this, and what does it mainly affect?
options: Systematic error, which affects accuracy
Random error, which affects precision
Systematic error, which affects precision
Random error, which affects accuracy
questions.explanation: An error that shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction is systematic, and it moves results away from the true value, reducing accuracy. Readings can still agree closely with each other, so precision is unaffected.

questions.stem: Students time a colour change by eye with a stopwatch, and their times vary by a second or two either way from trial to trial. How can the effect of this error best be reduced?
options: Use a stopwatch that displays time to 0.01 s instead of 0.1 s
Repeat the trials and calculate a mean time for each condition
Recalibrate the stopwatch against a clock before each trial
Record only the fastest time measured for each condition
questions.explanation: Variation in either direction is random error, here from judging the end point by eye and reaction time. Averaging repeated trials reduces its effect. A stopwatch with finer resolution does not help when the human judgement is the source of the error.

questions.stem: What is an extraneous variable?
options: The variable that is deliberately changed by the investigator during the experiment
The variable that is measured to find out the effect of changing the independent variable
A variable that has been shown to have no effect on the outcome of the experiment
Any variable other than the independent variable that could affect the dependent variable
questions.explanation: Extraneous variables are factors besides the independent variable that might influence the dependent variable, so they must be controlled or monitored. The variable that is changed is the independent variable, and the one measured is the dependent variable.

questions.stem: Students compare the growth of seedlings watered with tap water or rainwater. All the tap-water seedlings are on a top shelf near a heater. Why is temperature a confounding variable here?
options: It differs between the two groups, so its effect cannot be separated from that of water type
It was measured as the dependent variable instead of the growth of the seedlings
It changed randomly from day to day by the same amount for all of the seedlings
It is the independent variable, because heat changes how quickly seedlings grow
questions.explanation: A confounding variable is an extraneous variable that changes along with the independent variable. Because only the tap-water seedlings were warmer, any difference in growth could be due to temperature or to water type. Placing the trays randomly on the same shelf would fix this.

questions.stem: A ruler is marked in millimetres. Using the half-the-smallest-division convention, what is the uncertainty of a single reading?
options: ±1 cm
±5 mm
questions.explanation: For an analogue scale, the uncertainty of a reading is commonly taken as half the smallest division. The smallest division is 1 mm, so the uncertainty is ±0.5 mm.

questions.stem: Before using hydrochloric acid to treat a plant tissue sample, a student reads its safety data sheet (SDS). What will the SDS tell her?
options: Its hazards, safe handling and storage, first aid and disposal
The steps of a practical and the equipment that it requires
The concentrations a teacher should use for each year level
The results expected when it is used in a school experiment
questions.explanation: A safety data sheet, also called a material safety data sheet, sets out a substance's hazards and how to handle, store and dispose of it safely, with first aid measures. The steps of a task belong in a method or standard operating procedure.

questions.stem: After culturing microorganisms from swabs, how should the sealed agar plates be disposed of?
options: Opened and rinsed out in the sink before going in the bin
Placed unopened straight into the general rubbish bin at school
Opened outdoors so that sunlight can kill the microbes
Sterilised unopened, for example by autoclaving, before disposal
questions.explanation: Cultures may contain pathogens grown to high numbers, so plates should stay sealed and be sterilised, usually in an autoclave, before disposal. Opening plates releases spores and cells, and putting live cultures in general waste spreads them.

questions.stem: A school laboratory has a standard operating procedure (SOP) for using its autoclave. What is the purpose of this document?
options: To explain the scientific theory behind each experiment in a course
To set out agreed steps for a task so that it is done safely and consistently
To record the results of each experiment as it is being carried out
To list the hazards of every chemical stored in the school laboratory
questions.explanation: An SOP gives step-by-step instructions for a routine task, such as using an autoclave, so everyone does it the same safe way. Results are recorded in a logbook, and chemical hazards are listed on safety data sheets.

questions.stem: Researchers studying a disease replace some animal tests with cell cultures and computer models. Which of the three Rs of animal ethics does this apply?
options: Responsibility
Replacement
Reduction
Refinement
questions.explanation: The three Rs are replacement (using alternatives to animals), reduction (using fewer animals) and refinement (reducing pain and distress). Cell cultures and computer models replace animals, rather than reducing their number.

questions.stem: A microscope has a 15× eyepiece and a 40× objective lens. What is the total magnification?
questions.explanation: Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification = 15 × 40 = 600×. Adding the two values gives 55×, which is a common slip.

questions.stem: At a total magnification of 100×, the field of view is 2.0 mm in diameter. What is its diameter at 400×?
options: 5.0 mm
0.5 mm
8.0 mm
0.2 mm
questions.explanation: The diameter of the field of view is inversely proportional to magnification. Magnification increases four times, so the field of view becomes a quarter as wide: 2.0 ÷ 4 = 0.5 mm.

questions.stem: At 400× the field of view is 0.50 mm in diameter. About 10 cheek cells lie end to end across it. What is the approximate width of one cell?
options: 5 µm
500 µm
20 µm
50 µm
questions.explanation: Each cell is 0.50 mm ÷ 10 = 0.050 mm wide. Since 1 mm = 1000 µm, this is 0.050 × 1000 = 50 µm.

questions.stem: In a micrograph magnified 2000 times, a pollen grain is 40 mm across. What is its actual diameter?
options: 200 µm
80 µm
20 µm
2 µm
questions.explanation: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 40 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.020 mm. Multiplying by 1000 converts this to 20 µm. Multiplying the image size by the magnification gives an impossible result.

questions.stem: Which is a convention of biological scientific drawing?
options: Label structures with arrows drawn freehand across the drawing
Use clear, single lines with no shading, and label with ruled lines
Shade structures to show depth and add colour to show their identity
Draw every cell in the field of view using light, sketchy lines
questions.explanation: Scientific drawings use clean, continuous lines without shading or colour, with labels joined by straight ruled lines that do not cross. They also give a title and magnification. Drawing a few representative cells is better than every cell.

questions.stem: Which statement describes random sampling?
options: The researcher chooses the spots that look most typical of the area
Every point in the study area has an equal chance of being sampled
Samples are taken at regular intervals along a line across the area
The area is divided into zones and each zone is sampled separately
questions.explanation: In random sampling, positions are chosen without bias, for example from random number coordinates, so every point is equally likely to be sampled. Regular intervals describe systematic sampling, and sampling separate zones describes stratified sampling.

questions.stem: A study area is 70% grassland and 30% wetland. Researchers place 14 quadrats at random in the grassland and 6 at random in the wetland. Which sampling method is this?
options: Stratified sampling
Systematic sampling
Capture-recapture
Simple random sampling
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling divides an area into distinct zones (strata) and samples each one, here in proportion to its area. Simple random sampling would place all 20 quadrats at random across the whole area, ignoring the zones.

questions.stem: Which technique is most appropriate for studying how plant species change from a beach to the dunes behind it?
options: A single quadrat placed in the middle of the dunes
A belt transect running inland from the high-tide mark
Quadrats placed at random across the whole study area
Capture-recapture of the plants found along the shoreline
questions.explanation: A transect is used to study change along an environmental gradient, such as distance from the sea. Random quadrats would estimate overall abundance but would not show how the community changes with distance. Capture-recapture is for mobile animals.

questions.stem: What extra information does a belt transect give compared with a line transect?
options: The number of mobile animals that pass along the line during the survey
The exact age of each plant that touches the line along its whole length
The species found at one randomly chosen point in the middle of the line
The abundance of each species in quadrats along the line, not just presence
questions.explanation: A line transect records only the species touching the line at intervals. A belt transect places quadrats along the line, so abundance, density or percentage cover can be measured at each point along the gradient.

questions.stem: In a capture-recapture study, 24 skinks are caught, marked and released. A week later, 45 are caught, and 6 of them are marked. What is the estimated population size?
questions.explanation: Population size N = (number marked first × total caught second) ÷ number marked in second sample = (24 × 45) ÷ 6 = 180. The value 1080 forgets to divide by the recaptures.

questions.stem: In a capture-recapture study, some of the paint marks wear off the lizards before the second capture. How does this affect the population estimate?
options: The population is underestimated, because more unmarked animals are caught
The estimate is unaffected, because the second sample is still the same size
The population is overestimated, because fewer marked animals are recaptured
The population is underestimated, because fewer marked animals are recaptured
questions.explanation: Lost marks reduce the number of animals recognised as recaptures. Since the recapture number is the divisor in N = (M × C) ÷ R, a smaller value makes the estimate too large. The method assumes marks are not lost.

questions.stem: Five 0.25 m² quadrats contain 3, 5, 4, 0 and 8 sea stars. What is the mean density of sea stars?
options: 4 per m²
1 per m²
20 per m²
16 per m²
questions.explanation: Mean per quadrat = (3 + 5 + 4 + 0 + 8) ÷ 5 = 4 per 0.25 m². Each square metre holds four quadrats, so the density is 4 ÷ 0.25 = 16 per m². The value 4 forgets to convert to a square metre.

questions.stem: What does a large standard deviation indicate about a set of measurements?
options: The values are widely spread around the mean
The values are clustered closely around the mean
The mean is much larger than the median value
The sample size used was very large
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures how spread out values are from the mean. A large value shows wide variation; a small value shows the data are clustered near the mean.

questions.stem: A sample of 16 leaves has a standard deviation in length of 2.4 mm. What is the standard error of the mean?
options: 0.6 mm
9.6 mm
questions.explanation: Standard error = standard deviation ÷ √n = 2.4 ÷ √16 = 2.4 ÷ 4 = 0.6 mm. Dividing by n instead of √n gives 0.15 mm.

questions.stem: Why does the standard error of the mean get smaller as the sample size increases?
options: A larger sample gives a more reliable estimate of the population mean
A larger sample always has a smaller spread of individual values
A larger sample removes the systematic error from measurements
A larger sample makes the mean itself become a larger number
questions.explanation: Standard error is the standard deviation divided by √n, so it falls as n rises, showing the sample mean is a more reliable estimate of the true mean. The spread of individual values does not necessarily shrink, and systematic error is unaffected by sample size.

questions.stem: A column graph shows the mean heights of plants given fertiliser A and fertiliser B, with error bars of ±2 standard errors. The error bars overlap a great deal. What can be concluded?
options: The difference between the two means is unlikely to be significant
Fertiliser A is significantly better, because its mean is higher
The data are invalid, because error bars should never overlap
Neither fertiliser had any effect at all on plant height
questions.explanation: Widely overlapping error bars of ±2 SE suggest the difference between the means could be due to chance, so it is unlikely to be statistically significant. Without a control group of unfertilised plants, nothing can be said about whether either fertiliser had an effect.

questions.stem: A t-test comparing the mean leaf area of plants in sun and in shade gives p = 0.02. Using a significance level of 0.05, what should be concluded?
options: Accept the null hypothesis: there is a 98% chance that the means are the same
Reject the null hypothesis: the difference in means is statistically significant
Accept the null hypothesis: the difference in means is not statistically significant
Reject the null hypothesis: leaves in shade are exactly 2% larger than in sun
questions.explanation: When p is less than 0.05, a difference this large would be unlikely if there were no real difference, so the null hypothesis is rejected and the difference is significant. The p-value is a probability, not the size of the difference.

questions.stem: When is Spearman's rank correlation coefficient preferred to Pearson's correlation coefficient?
options: When the means of two separate groups are compared to find a difference
When only one variable has been measured for each individual sampled
When the data are ranks, or the relationship is monotonic but not linear
When the data are normally distributed and the relationship is linear
questions.explanation: Spearman's rank tests whether one variable consistently increases or decreases with another, using ranked data, so it suits non-linear or non-normal data. Pearson's coefficient measures the strength of a linear relationship. Comparing two group means calls for a t-test.

questions.stem: A study finds Pearson's r = −0.92 between soil salinity and plant height. Which statement describes this result?
options: A weak negative correlation: height tends to fall as salinity rises
A strong positive correlation: height tends to rise as salinity rises
Proof that the salinity of the soil causes the fall in plant height
A strong negative correlation: height tends to fall as salinity rises
questions.explanation: An r value close to −1 indicates a strong negative linear relationship. Correlation alone does not show causation, because another factor, such as waterlogging, might affect both variables.

questions.stem: A trendline on a scatterplot of transpiration rate against light intensity has R² = 0.81. What does this value mean?
options: Exactly 81% of the data points lie on the trendline drawn on the scatterplot
There is an 81% chance that light intensity causes the rate of transpiration
About 81% of the variation in transpiration rate is explained by the trendline
Transpiration rate increases by 0.81 units for every unit increase in light
questions.explanation: R² is the coefficient of determination: the proportion of variation in the dependent variable accounted for by the trendline. The rise per unit of light is the gradient, not R², and R² says nothing about causation.

questions.stem: Which graph best presents the mean dry mass of seedlings grown with four different fertiliser brands, showing variability?
options: A scatterplot of the means with a trendline and R²
A line graph joining the four means in order
A pie chart of the total mass for each brand
A column graph of the means with error bars
questions.explanation: Fertiliser brand is a categorical independent variable, so a column graph is appropriate, and error bars show variability. Line graphs and scatterplots with trendlines are for continuous independent variables.

questions.stem: Students estimate photosynthesis rate by counting bubbles from pondweed. Results are consistent across repeats, but tests show much of the gas is dissolved air released as the water warms. How is the method best described?
options: Both valid and reliable, because the results were consistent across all of the repeats
Neither valid nor reliable, because the repeated trials did not agree with each other
Reliable but not valid, because it does not measure only the oxygen from photosynthesis
Valid but not reliable, because the bubbles produced vary in size from trial to trial
questions.explanation: The results were consistent, so the method is reliable. But the bubbles include air released by warming, so the method does not measure what it claims to, and it is not valid. Consistency alone does not make a method valid.

questions.stem: The true concentration of a nitrate standard is 5.0 mg/L. A student's test kit gives readings of 6.1, 6.0, 6.1 and 6.2 mg/L. How should the readings be described?
options: Both accurate and precise
Neither accurate nor precise
Precise but not accurate
Accurate but not precise
questions.explanation: The readings agree closely with each other, so they are precise, but they are all about 1 mg/L above the true value, so they are not accurate. This pattern points to a systematic error in the kit.

questions.stem: Which source would be the most credible evidence about the safety of a new vaccine?
options: A peer-reviewed journal article reporting a large clinical trial
A manufacturer's advertisement summarising its own trial results
A popular blog by a parent describing their child's experience
A news article quoting one doctor's personal opinion on the vaccine
questions.explanation: Peer-reviewed research reporting a large trial has had its methods and conclusions checked by independent experts, and a large sample improves reliability. Advertisements may be biased, and single experiences or opinions are anecdotal.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of peer review in science?
options: The authors repeat their own experiment to confirm their results before publishing
Members of the public vote on whether a study's conclusions should be accepted
A government agency decides whether a study should receive research funding
Independent experts check a study's methods and conclusions before it is published
questions.explanation: In peer review, scientists who are expert in the field, and independent of the study, evaluate its methods, analysis and conclusions before publication. This helps to catch errors and unsupported claims.
